entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Jan Žižka z Trocnova a Kalicha (c. 1360 – October 11, 1424) emerged from a minor Bohemian noble family to become one of medieval Europe's most innovative and feared military commanders. A fervent follower of the theologian Jan Hus, Žižka galvanized the radical Taborite faction of the Hussite movement, transforming a religious uprising into a formidable military force that defied the Holy Roman Empire and papal authority. His strategic genius and tactical innovations fundamentally altered warfare in Central Europe, establishing the Kingdom of Bohemia as a bastion of religious reform and national identity against overwhelming crusading armies, thereby shaping the political and religious landscape of the 15th century.

Žižka's military career, ignited by Jan Hus’s execution in 1415, saw him lead the Hussites to a series of astonishing victories that reshaped tactical doctrine. Despite losing an eye early in the Hussite Wars, and later the other, he masterminded campaigns that repeatedly crushed crusader forces, notably at Sudoměř (1420) and Vítkov Hill (1420) where his use of Wagenburg (wagon fort) tactics proved decisive. His strategic brilliance was further demonstrated in the rout of Sigismund's forces at Kutná Hora (1421) and Německý Brod (1422), securing Bohemian autonomy and demonstrating the potency of a disciplined, religiously motivated citizen army against traditional feudal levies.

entities.summary:
Jan Žižka z Trocnova a Kalicha (c. 1360–1424) was a formidable Czech military commander and a central figure of the Radical Hussite movement, leading the Taborite faction through a period of intense religious and political upheaval in Bohemia from 1419 until his death. A contemporary and fervent follower of the reformer Jan Hus, Žižka transformed a disparate group of peasants and townsfolk into an disciplined and innovative fighting force, successfully defending Hussite Bohemia against five crusades launched by the Holy Roman Empire and the Papacy. His unwavering commitment to the Hussite cause and his unparalleled tactical genius fundamentally shaped the trajectory of Central European history in the early 15th century, securing a temporary religious autonomy for Bohemia.

Žižka's military career, notably marked by his undefeated record, revolutionized medieval warfare through the pioneering development of the *wagenburg* (wagon fort) and the effective integration of gunpowder artillery with infantry tactics. Key victories include the Battle of Sudoměř (1420), where his forces repelled Catholic knights despite being outnumbered, and the decisive Battle of Vítkov Hill (1420), which secured Prague against a crusader siege. Even after losing one eye early in the wars and later becoming completely blind at the Siege of Rabí in 1421, Žižka continued to command his armies with remarkable success, dictating strategy and maneuvers through his lieutenants, culminating in the rout of Sigismund's forces at the Battle of Německý Brod in 1422.
